html:
Wong Ka Kui, the frontman of the Hong Kong rock band Beyond, and Freddie Mercury, the frontman of Queen.

That gives my age away completely.

I started listening to Beyond in ninth grade and have kept at it ever since: sixteen years now. The first song I heard was “Silent Years,” and I thought, what on earth is this? Later, somehow, I came across “Really Love You” and was hooked on the spot. I borrowed a classmate’s VCD and never gave it back; whenever he asked, I said I’d lost it… It was the classic 1991 concert. Back then my afternoon nap was sacred to me, but every so often I’d pick a lunchtime to skip it and watch the whole VCD, and then spend the afternoon desperately sleepy. Because of Beyond, I bought a guitar as soon as the college entrance exam was over, and I’ve played on and off ever since. My biggest dream is to go out on the street and sing their songs at the top of my lungs. It sounds like a line from The Voice of China. There are lots of good songs and lots of good singers, of course. But what makes me truly love Beyond, besides a sigh for Ka Kui’s legendary life, is the band’s attitude to music, to living and to life itself. After all the lovey-dovey drivel, Beyond is a real eye-opener, like suddenly seeing hope in life. You tire of every song eventually, and Beyond’s are no exception. But the magic is that every so often I dig them out again, listen to them obsessively and get fired up all over again. Later I also liked Jay Chou and other heartthrob singers, but nobody has ever taken Beyond’s place.

That same mania for Beyond didn’t come back until last year, when I watched Bohemian Rhapsody and went all in on Queen, just as fervently as back then. I listened to all their songs and watched the documentaries, the behind-the-scenes stories and so on.

I found that Beyond and Queen have a surprising amount in common: original rock bands, varied and virile music, frontmen who died young. If there’s a difference, it’s that Beyond makes you angry and makes you think, while Queen gives you strength. Music, like writing, doesn’t go out of date. It endures, like Ka Kui and Freddie, and their spirit lives on.
